title: Checkpoint: Governments and Money
objective: After this level you can explain how taxes, spending and central banks shape an economy.
summary: Fiscal policy is spending and taxing by elected governments; monetary policy is the central bank steering rates and money. Chapter 6 in two levers.

cards.headline: Two sets of hands steer an economy, and they sit in different buildings.
cards.body: In the US, one set belongs to Congress and the President, the other to the Federal Reserve. Chapter 6 has shown you both at work. Time to give them their names.

cards.headline: Fiscal policy: spending and taxing
cards.body: Fiscal policy means a government's spending and taxing decisions; in the US, Congress and the administration make them. It covers most of this chapter: Level 51's taxes, Level 52's question of who pays, Level 53's public goods, Level 54's deficits and debt, and Level 59's safety nets.

cards.headline: Monetary policy: rates and money
cards.body: Monetary policy is what a central bank does, mainly with interest rates, to pursue goals like stable prices and maximum employment. That was Levels 55–57. The two jobs are kept apart. The Federal Reserve plays no role in setting taxes or government spending.

mascot.line: Easy to mix up: fiscal is who taxes and spends; monetary is who steers interest rates.

items.label: Monetary policy
points: Example: raising rates to cool prices

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How governments steer an economy with two separate levers: taxing and spending, and interest rates.
Why a raise never cuts your take-home pay, and how progressive, flat and regressive taxes differ.
What separates one year's deficit from the national debt, and why economists weigh debt differently.
How a central bank's key rate cools or speeds up spending, and why the effect arrives late.

questions.prompt: In the US, who makes fiscal policy?

options.label: The Federal Reserve
options.rationale: The Fed makes monetary policy and plays no role in fiscal policy.

options.label: Commercial banks
options.rationale: Banks follow rules; they do not set taxes or spending.

options.label: Congress and the administration
The OECD
options.rationale: The OECD compares countries; it does not set their budgets.

questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxing, decided by Congress and the administration.

questions.prompt: Which of these is monetary policy rather than fiscal policy?

options.label: Cutting income tax rates
Raising the central bank's key interest rate
Building new highways
Borrowing to cover a budget deficit
options.rationale: Government borrowing is part of fiscal policy.

questions.explanation: Interest rates are the central bank's tool; taxes, spending and borrowing are the government's.

questions.prompt: From Level 52: which argument do supporters of a flat income tax make?

options.label: It is simpler and encourages working, saving and investing
It takes a bigger share from higher incomes
It is guaranteed to raise more revenue
options.rationale: Critics argue it could raise less.

options.label: It removes all taxes on spending
options.rationale: A flat income tax says nothing about sales taxes.

questions.explanation: Supporters stress simplicity and incentives; critics stress fairness and revenue.

questions.prompt: From Level 54: what do economists mean by "crowding out"?

options.label: Too many people using a public good at once
options.rationale: That would be about rivalry, not borrowing.

options.label: Government borrowing leaving less money for private investment
Banks refusing to hold capital
options.rationale: Capital rules are a different topic, from Level 58.

options.label: Taxes pushing shoppers out of stores
options.rationale: Crowding out is about borrowing and investment.

questions.explanation: Heavy government borrowing can soak up savings, leaving less for private investment. Others note borrowing can fund growth-boosting investment.

questions.prompt: From Level 59: what did Germany pioneer in 1889?

options.label: The first central bank
The first value-added tax
The first flat income tax in Eastern Europe
The first old-age social insurance

questions.explanation: Under Bismarck, Germany became the first nation with old-age social insurance, paying from age 70.
